newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Lloyd's survives surgery, but faces more upheaval.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Lloyd's survives surgery, but faces more upheaval.

text.p: Lloyd's of London has effected radical changes to save itself from the threat of collapse, but the more gradual process of evolution could yet see the insurance market alter beyond all recognition.

In a few short weeks, Lloyd's has cast off the problems that have beset it for the past five years and is now gearing itself up to expand and modernise after years of damage limitation and limping from crisis to catastrophe.

The market has signed a peace treaty with its traditional supporters for an end to litigation, passed its annual solvency test and gained regulatory approval for the Equitas reinsurance company to take on responsibility for old liabilities.

The implementation of these key planks of its reconstruction and renewal (R&R) plan means that the world's oldest insurance market has survived record losses of more than eight billion pounds ($12.45 billion), the threat of bankruptcy, a tidal wave of litigation, allegations of negligence and worse.
However, in its odyssey out of the wilderness of losses and litigation, Lloyd's has already shed many of the things which made it unique and the forces of change show no sign of abating.
LIMITED LIABILITY

Lloyd's has allowed in corporate investors for the first time in its 300-year history and with them limited liability, thereby giving up the famous "unlimited liability" boast of its traditional individual backers known as Names.
"There will be a few Names who want to continue with unlimited liability, but that will decrease over time," said one members' agent, a species itself on the danger list as Names' numbers dwindle.
The number of members' agencies, which provide a similar service to equity market stockbrokers, is expected to decline through rationalisation to 10 or 15 from the current 30.
However, the remaining members' agencies argue they will still have a role to play, as will private investors, in the reconstructed Lloyd's.

"Lloyd's needs investors with a long term view. The short term view of the institutional investor doesn't fit very well in the Lloyd's environment with its cycles over quite a long period," said one members' agent.
CONSOLIDATION

Consolidation and rationalisation have scythed through the whole market since the early 1990s, slashing the number of underwriting syndicates to 170 from a peak of 400 and active Names to 13,000 from 34,000.

Radical change became necessary after the record losses that hit the market in the early 1990s following a combination of man-made and natural disasters, which were exacerbated by negligence and mismanagement within Lloyd's.

The losses wiped out the assets of thousands of Names, led many others to quit and posed the market the problem of finding a replacement source of capital, while keeping surviving Names on side for the time being.
"You aren't going to get anyone else wanting to be a Name, but those still there won't leave so fast," said one observer.
NEW MONEY

Having moved off the critical list, Lloyd's now faces a battle for control of the market between Names and institutional investors. How long Names remain the majority providers of capital to Lloyd's is crucial to their survival.

"Names have stayed, but I suspect there will be further discussion and arguments about the place of Names within the market and some Names may well fight back against the spread of corporate capital," one Lloyd's analyst said.
For the 1996 year, Names provided 70 percent of Lloyd's 9.97 billion pound capacity -- the amount of premium income the market can write -- but corporates are growing year by year.

"If Names fall below 50 percent of capacity, they will no longer dominate decision making at Lloyd's, which will be run by and for limited liability corporate investors," Oliver Carruthers of the High Premium Group of Names said.

With no new Names joining the market, their days are probably numbered. Members' agents and others are developing ways to keep existing Names and lure new individual investors to the market, but these will only be available from 1998.
"I think it'll carry on for the next few years as a very mixed market. Longer term it's more difficult to tell, when you get to such a fundamental evolution," said one market source.
INDEPENDENCE

This conflict is bound up with the struggle between the tradition of the semi-autonomous Lloyd's underwriters, who provide the market's core insurance skills, and those who say they should be more tightly controlled.
Managing agents, who run syndicates, are at the centre of a maelstrom of change as they try to secure new sources of long term capital and create more cost-effective structures.

"There's quite a lot of consolidation in the pipeline... Managing agents are being bought by U.S. and Bermudan companies, others by listed corporate investors, and I'd expect that process to continue," one analyst said.
These corporate changes are likely to curb the independence of underwriters and impose on them the kind of controls exercised by large insurance companies.

Underwriters say tighter control threatens their ability to make quick decisions and develop new products as well as Lloyd's reputation for insuring the bizarre -- from actresses' legs to impregnation by aliens.
STRENGTHS

However, Lloyd's participants agree that two unique aspects of the market are worth defending -- the Central Fund, a mutual guarantee fund backing all Lloyd's policies, and the licences obtained centrally which allow syndicates and brokers to operate around the world.

"If Lloyd's changes fundamentally from being the innovative, entrepreneurial sort of place where there's collective security, I don't know whether we'd compete that well with the world's giants," said Bryan Kellett, chairman of Archer Group, one of the largest Lloyd's managing agencies.

"It's better if we do all those sorts of things together, open doors, together. Individually, the syndicates are not that big, but if you look at the thing collectively, we're a big organisation. That's one of the strengths that we shouldn't give up lightly," he added. ($1=.6430 Pound)
